claim: 94.1 ± 2.5% of GFP-labeled cells in the dentate gyrus of SOM-GFP transgenic mice expressed somatostatin (SOM+).
source: Confocal image stacks revealed that 94.1 ± 2.5% of GFP-labeled cells expressed SOM (SOM+; Figure 1B; three mice, six slices / mouse; dorsal and ventral DG).
evidence: Based on confocal microscopy data from three mice with six slices per mouse examining both dorsal and ventral DG regions.

claim: 62.8 ± 4.8% of SOM-Cy3-labeled cells co-localized GFP in the dentate gyrus of SOM-GFP transgenic mice.
source: Consistent with previous reports in CA1 and CA3 (Oliva et al., 2000), only a fraction of SOM-Cy3-labeled cells co-localized GFP (62.8 ± 4.8%; Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on confocal microscopy data and consistent with previous reports by Oliva et al., 2000.

claim: GFP-expression is a reliable marker for SOM+ cells in the dentate gyrus.
source: Thus, GFP-expression is a reliable marker for SOM+ cells in the DG.
evidence: Inferred from the high colocalization rate (94.1%) of GFP with SOM.

claim: HIPP cells have axon fibers distributed in the molecular layer with the highest proportion (74.7 ± 2.1%) in the outer molecular layer.
source: One group of DG-SOMIs had HIPP morphologies (Halasy and Somogyi, 1993; Han et al., 1993; Hosp et al., 2014; Savanthrapadian et al., 2014) with axon fibers distributed in the molecular layer with highest proportion in the outer molecular layer (74.7 ± 2.1%; six reconstructed cells; Figure 1C,E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on morphological reconstructions of six HIPP cells and consistent with previous reports.

claim: HIPP cells project 1.7 ± 1.1% of their axon fibers in the hilus.
source: Some axon fibres projected in the hilus (1.7 ± 1.1%, Figure 1C,E) consistent with our recent observation that HIPPs are interconnected by perisomatic synapses (Savanthrapadian et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on morphological reconstructions and consistent with previous observations by Savanthrapadian et al., 2014.

claim: HIL cells project almost exclusively in the hilus (91.0 ± 1.7% of the total axonal length).
source: In marked contrast, the second group of recorded SOMIs projected almost exclusively in the hilus (91.0 ± 1.7% of the total axonal length; six reconstructed cells) and were therefore termed hilus-associated interneurons (HILs; Figure 1C, right; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on morphological reconstructions of six HIL cells.

claim: Both HIPP and HIL cells largely avoid the granule cell layer (HIPP 3.9 ± 0.6%, HIL 2.1 ± 0.8% of the total axonal length).
source: Both cell types largely avoided the granule cell layer (HIPP 3.9 ± 0.6%, HIL 2.1 ± 0.8% of the total axonal length; Figure 1E).
evidence: Based on morphological reconstructions showing axonal distribution patterns.

claim: The total dendritic length is similar between HIPP and HIL cells (HIPP 2500.4 ± 333.0 µm, HIL 2547.3 ± 427.8 µm, p=0.935).
source: Despite the marked layer-specific axonal dispersion, the total dendritic and axonal length in the DG was similar among both types (dendrite: HIPP 2500.4 ± 333.0 µm, HIL 2547.3 ± 427.8 µm, p=0.935, t-test; axon: HIPP 26.8 ± 4.0 mm, HIL 20.7 ± 2.5 mm, p=0.205, t-test; Figure 1D).
evidence: Based on morphological reconstructions with statistical comparison using t-test.

claim: The total axonal length is similar between HIPP and HIL cells (HIPP 26.8 ± 4.0 mm, HIL 20.7 ± 2.5 mm, p=0.205).
source: Despite the marked layer-specific axonal dispersion, the total dendritic and axonal length in the DG was similar among both types (dendrite: HIPP 2500.4 ± 333.0 µm, HIL 2547.3 ± 427.8 µm, p=0.935, t-test; axon: HIPP 26.8 ± 4.0 mm, HIL 20.7 ± 2.5 mm, p=0.205, t-test; Figure 1D).
evidence: Based on morphological reconstructions with statistical comparison using t-test.

claim: The majority of identified HIPP and HIL cells (33 out of 35 cells) expressed somatostatin as confirmed by antibody labelling.
source: Antibody labelling revealed that the majority of identified HIPP and HIL cells in this study fulfilled the criterion of SOM-expression (33 out of 35 cells; Figure 1A, inset).
evidence: Based on antibody labeling experiments confirming SOM expression.

claim: Both HIPP and HIL neuron types were morphologically and physiologically identified in SOM-tdT mice, confirming their strain-independent occurrence.
source: Finally, both neuron types were morphologically and physiologically identified in SOM-tdT mice (SOM-Cre x Ai9-RCL-tdT; Materials and methods) confirming their strain-independent occurrence (seven light-microscopically identified HIPP and 7 HIL cells).
evidence: Based on identification in a different mouse strain (SOM-tdT mice).

claim: The membrane capacitance is similar between HIPP and HIL cells (HIPP 47.8 ± 6.3 pF, HIL 50.5 ± 2.4 pF; p=0.63).
source: Consistent with their comparable dendritic and axonal length in the DG, we observed no difference in the membrane capacitance (HIPP 47.8 ± 6.3 pF, 7 cells; HIL 50.5 ± 2.4 pF, 22 cells; p=0.63).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological measurements from 7 HIPP and 22 HIL cells.

claim: The membrane resting potential is similar between HIPP and HIL cells (HIPP −54.2 ± 1.0 mV, HIL −57.1 ± 1.1 mV; p=0.079).
source: The membrane resting potential was also similar (HIPP −54.2 ± 1.0 mV, 14 cells; HIL −57.1 ± 1.1 mV, 22 cells; p=0.079, t-test; Figure 1F).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological measurements from 14 HIPP and 22 HIL cells with statistical comparison using t-test.

claim: HIPP cells have a ~1.5 times slower membrane time constant than HIL cells (HIPP 14.3 ± 1.4 ms, HIL 9.3 ± 0.6 ms; p<0.001).
source: However, HIPPs had a ~ 1.5 times slower membrane time constant (τm) and a ~1.7 times higher input resistance than HILs (τm: HIPP 14.3 ± 1.4 ms, HIL 9.3 ± 0.6 ms; p<0.001; input resistance: HIPP 317.9 ± 34.0 MΩ, 8 cells; HIL 186.7 ± 12.1 MΩ, 24 cells; p<0.001; t-test; Figure 1G,H).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological measurements with statistical comparison using t-test.

claim: HIPP cells have a ~1.7 times higher input resistance than HIL cells (HIPP 317.9 ± 34.0 MΩ, HIL 186.7 ± 12.1 MΩ; p<0.001).
source: However, HIPPs had a ~ 1.5 times slower membrane time constant (τm) and a ~1.7 times higher input resistance than HILs (τm: HIPP 14.3 ± 1.4 ms, HIL 9.3 ± 0.6 ms; p<0.001; input resistance: HIPP 317.9 ± 34.0 MΩ, 8 cells; HIL 186.7 ± 12.1 MΩ, 24 cells; p<0.001; t-test; Figure 1G,H).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological measurements from 8 HIPP and 24 HIL cells with statistical comparison using t-test.

claim: The half-duration of single action potentials is longer for HIPP than for HIL cells (0.86 ± 0.08 ms vs 0.62 ± 0.03 ms; p<0.001).
source: Moreover, the half-duration of single action potentials was longer for HIPP than for HIL cells (0.86 ± 0.08 ms vs 0.62 ± 0.03 ms; p<0.001, t-test; Figure 1I; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological measurements with statistical comparison using t-test.

claim: The slope in the decay of single action potentials is larger in HIL cells than in HIPP cells (HIPP 122.0 ± 10.9 mV ms−1, HIL 183.3 ± 9.8 mV ms−1; p=0.003).
source: The narrower spike width in HILs was correlated with a larger slope in the decay of single action potentials (HIPP 122.0 ± 10.9 mV ms−1, HIL 183.3 ± 9.8 mV ms−1; p=0.003, t-test; Figure 1J, left) suggesting a different expression profile of voltage-gated channels in the two SOMI types.
evidence: Based on electrophysiological measurements with statistical comparison using t-test, suggesting different voltage-gated channel expression.

claim: The maximal discharge frequency is lower for HIPP than for HIL cells (111.4 ± 10.2 Hz vs 141.5 ± 5.7 Hz; p=0.015).
source: Furthermore, disparities were observed in activity patterns evoked by long-lasting positive current injections with step-wise increasing amplitudes. The maximal discharge frequency was lower for HIPP than for HIL cells (111.4 ± 10.2 Hz vs 141.5 ± 5.7 Hz; p=0.015, t-test; Figure 1J, right).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological measurements with statistical comparison using t-test.

claim: The ratio between the last and the first inter-spike-intervals at maximal discharge frequency is higher for HIPP cells (2.1 ± 0.09) than for HIL cells (1.6 ± 0.12; p=0.004), indicating stronger adaptation of spike trains in HIPP cells.
source: Moreover, the ratio between the last and the first inter-spike-intervals at maximal discharge frequency was higher for HIPPs (2.1 ± 0.09) indicating a stronger adaptation of spike trains than for HIL cells (1.6 ± 0.12; p=0.004, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological measurements with statistical comparison using Mann-Whitney U test.

claim: Hierarchical cluster analysis based on morphological and physiological parameters reveals that DG-SOMIs fall into two distinct classes corresponding to HIPP and HIL cells.
source: To further test whether DG-SOMIs can be classified into independent types, we performed a hierarchical cluster analysis on the basis of morphological variables obtained from the fully reconstructed interneurons and their passive and active membrane characteristics (Figure 1K; depicted as triangles in Figure 1F–J; Materials and methods). We found that interneurons fell into two classes separated by an Euclidian linkage distance of 25% (Figure 1K). The first cluster was formed by slow signaling HIPP cells with axon collaterals largely located in the outer molecular layer, whereas the second cluster was formed by fast-spiking HIL cells with axon collaterals largely constrained to the hilus.
evidence: Based on hierarchical cluster analysis of morphological and physiological data from reconstructed cells.

claim: Cre-induced GFP-expression in SOM-Cre mice is highly specific, with 95.4 ± 3.2% co-localization with somatostatin.
source: Cre-induced GFP-expression was highly specific as confirmed by antibody labeling against SOM (95.4 ± 3.2% co-localization; seven slices, three mice; Figure 2A,C).
evidence: Based on antibody labeling experiments in seven slices from three mice.

claim: GFP-expressing cell bodies in SOM-Cre mice injected with rAAV-FLEX-GFP are restricted to the hilus.
source: Moreover, GFP-expressing cell bodies were restricted to the hilus, defined as the area between the granule cell layer and the pyramidal cell layer of CA3 (see Figure 1C left, black dashed line), in line with earlier immunohistochemical reports (Acsády et al., 2000; Peng et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on confocal microscopy observations consistent with previous reports by Acsády et al., 2000 and Peng et al., 2013.

claim: GFP+ axonal fibers from DG-SOMIs are found in the hilus and the molecular layer but rarely in the granule cell layer.
source: GFP+ axonal fibers were found in the hilus and the molecular layer but rarely in the granule cell layer confirming the spatial specificity of the DG injection site (Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on confocal microscopy observations of axonal fiber distribution.

claim: SOM+ axon collaterals from the dentate gyrus project to the hippocampal fissure and along the fimbria to the medial septum and the vertical limb of the diagonal band of Broca (MSvDB).
source: Three-dimensional-images of clarity-processed whole mounts of injected brains (Materials and methods) showed that SOM+ axon collaterals projected to the hippocampal fissure and along the fimbria to the medial septum and the vertical limb of the diagonal band of Broca (MSvDB; Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on 3D imaging of clarity-processed whole mount brains.

claim: 26.5 ± 2.4% of SOM-expressing cells in the dentate gyrus and hippocampus were retrogradely labeled with RedRetroBead after injection into the MSvDB.
source: After 3–8 days, we identified numerous red labeled cell bodies located in the hilus as well as in the stratum oriens and radiatum of CA1 and CA3 (26.5 ± 2.4% of SOM-expressing cells were labeled with RedRetroBead, 106 SOM cells; seven slices, two mice), confirming previous data on hippocampal-septal projecting SOMIs (Jinno and Kosaka, 2002; Gulyás et al., 2003).
evidence: Based on retrograde tracing experiments in seven slices from two mice, consistent with previous reports by Jinno and Kosaka, 2002 and Gulyás et al., 2003.

claim: Virtually all retrogradely tagged DG-septal projecting neurons expressed somatostatin (93.4 ± 2.2%).
source: Colocalization analysis revealed that cell bodies of virtually all retrogradely tagged DG-septal projecting neurons expressed SOM (93.4 ± 2.2%; seven slices, two mice; Figure 2C, right).
evidence: Based on colocalization analysis in seven slices from two mice.

claim: The majority (86.7%) of retrogradely tagged DG-septal projecting neurons are HIL cells with axon collaterals located in the hilus.
source: Whole-cell recordings of the tagged cells revealed that the majority of intracellularly labeled neurons had axon collaterals located in the hilus (86.7%; 13 HILs and 2 SOMIs with axon in the hilus and inner molecular layer; Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on whole-cell recordings and morphological analysis of 15 retrogradely labeled cells.

claim: None of the retrogradely labeled DG-septal projecting cells had axon fibers in the outer molecular layer.
source: None of the labeled cells had axon fibers in the outer molecular layer.
evidence: Based on morphological analysis of retrogradely labeled cells.

claim: HIL cells form the major anatomical substrate for long-distance DG-septal projections.
source: Thus, our data indicate that HIL cells form the major anatomical substrate for long-distance DG-septal projections.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that 86.7% of retrogradely labeled DG-septal cells are HIL cells.

claim: EPSCs recorded in HIPP cells can be substantially reduced by DCG-IV (by 51.7 ± 3.9%), indicating their mossy fiber-mediated nature.
source: EPSCs recorded in HIPPs could be substantially reduced by DCG-IV (by 51.7 ± 3.9%, 10 cells; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), indicating their mossy fiber-mediated nature.
evidence: Based on pharmacological experiments in 10 HIPP cells using DCG-IV, a selective blocker of mossy fiber synapses.

claim: EPSCs recorded in HIL cells are reduced by DCG-IV to a lesser mean extent (by 32.6 ± 9.4%) than in HIPP cells, but with high variability (range −2.4–96.0%).
source: EPSCs recorded in HIL cells were also diminished by DCG-IV, but to a much lesser mean extent (by 32.6 ± 9.4%, 16 cells; p=0.087, t-test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). More importantly, the magnitude of the DCG-IV effect was highly variable in HIL neurons (range −2.4–96.0%), more variable than in HIPP cells (range 34.1–78.1%; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on pharmacological experiments in 16 HIL cells using DCG-IV.

claim: A substantial proportion of HIL cells (10 out of 16) showed no or only mild DCG-IV effects (by <20%).
source: Indeed, a substantial proportion of HIL cells showed no or only mild DCG-IV effects (by <20%; 10 out of 16 cells).
evidence: Based on pharmacological experiments in 16 HIL cells.

claim: Both HIPP and HIL cells are targeted by mossy fibers, and HIL cells are preferentially targeted by additional excitatory inputs of different origin, very likely mossy cells.
source: Thus, our data indicate that both SOMI types are targeted by mossy fibers and HIL cells are preferentially targeted by additional excitatory inputs of different origin, very likely mossy cells (Larimer and Strowbridge, 2008).
evidence: Inferred from DCG-IV sensitivity data and consistent with previous reports by Larimer and Strowbridge, 2008.

claim: Associative burst frequency stimulation (aBFS) results in post-tetanic potentiation (PTP) followed by long-lasting depression (LTD) of synaptically evoked EPSCs in HIPP cells (PTP 176.2 ± 30.6%, LTD 65.1 ± 17.3% from baseline amplitude; p=0.01).
source: Application of the aBFS resulted in a post-tetanic potentiation (PTP) followed by long-lasting depression of synaptically evoked EPSCs in HIPP cells (PTP 176.2 ± 30.6%, mean LTD 15–20 min after aBFS 65.1 ± 17.3% from baseline amplitude; five out of seven recorded HIPP cells showed plastic changes; p=0.01, paired t-test; Figure 3A,B,E).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological plasticity experiments in 7 HIPP cells with statistical comparison using paired t-test.

claim: EPSCs in HIPP cells after LTD induction are substantially blocked by DCG-IV (52.3 ± 7.7%), indicating their mossy fiber-mediated nature.
source: EPSCs were substantially blocked after LTD induction by DCG-IV indicating their mossy fiber-mediated nature (52.3 ± 7.7%, range 34.1–78.1; five out of five cells; Figure 3F).
evidence: Based on pharmacological experiments in 5 HIPP cells after LTD induction.

claim: Associative burst frequency stimulation (aBFS) results in post-tetanic potentiation (PTP) followed by long-lasting potentiation (LTP) of synaptic responses in HIL cells (PTP 203.6 ± 20.4%, LTP 153.1 ± 14.9%; p=0.002).
source: In marked contrast, the same aBFS resulted in a PTP followed by a long-lasting potentiation of synaptic responses in HIL cells (PTP 203.6 ± 20.4% of baseline amplitude, p<0.001, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum test; mean LTP 153.1 ± 14.9%; 11 out of 12 recorded HIL cells showed plastic changes, p=0.002, paired t-test; Figure 3C,D,E).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological plasticity experiments in 12 HIL cells with statistical comparison using Mann-Whitney Rank Sum test and paired t-test.

claim: Potentiated EPSCs in HIL cells can be reduced by DCG-IV with high variability among individual cells (by 32.5 ± 9.9%, range −2.4–96.0%).
source: Potentiated EPSCs could be reduced by DCG-IV; however, the blocking effect was highly variable among individual HIL cells (by 32.5 ± 9.9%, range −2.4–96.0%, 11 cells; Figure 3F) suggesting that LTP was induced at mossy fiber terminals and at other glutamatergic synapses, very likely those originating from mossy cells (Larimer and Strowbridge, 2008).
evidence: Based on pharmacological experiments in 11 HIL cells after LTP induction, suggesting involvement of both mossy fiber and mossy cell inputs.

claim: The magnitude of synaptic plasticity (LTD/LTP) is not correlated with the extent of the DCG-IV blocking effect on synaptic transmission.
source: To examine whether plastic changes may depend on the nature of the input synapse, we plotted the magnitude of synaptic plasticity as a function of the DCG-IV blocking effect (Figure 3F, right). Both the magnitude of long-lasting depression and the potentiation of synaptic transmission were not correlated with the extent in the blocking effect of DCG-IV on synaptic transmission (Spearman Rank order Correlation, p>0.05 for both comparisons; Figure 3F, right).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis of plasticity magnitude and DCG-IV effects.

claim: The input resistance of recorded cells remains stable throughout plasticity experiments (LTD: baseline 326.3 ± 21.2 MΩ vs 15–20 min after LTD: 323.0 ± 25.5 MΩ; LTP: baseline 201.5 ± 19.2 MΩ vs after LTP: 204.8 ± 14.6 MΩ; p>0.05 for both).
source: Moreover, the magnitude of synaptic plasticity was not related to changes in the input resistance of the recorded cells. Indeed, the input resistance was stable throughout the entire recording periods (LTD: baseline 326.3 ± 21.2 MΩ vs 15–20 min after LTD expression: 323.0 ± 25.5 MΩ, 7 cells; LTP: 201.5 ± 19.2 MΩ vs after LTP expression: 204.8 ± 14.6 MΩ, 9 cells; p>0.05, paired t-test for both comparisons; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological measurements during plasticity experiments in 7 LTD and 9 LTP cells.

claim: The sign and magnitude of synaptic plasticity are not related to the peak amplitude of EPSCs obtained during control periods (LTD: baseline EPSC 77.0 ± 19.6 pA; LTP: baseline EPSC 74.6 ± 16.4 pA; p=0.767).
source: Finally, the sign and magnitude of synaptic plasticity were not related to the peak amplitude of EPSCs obtained during control periods (LTD: baseline EPSC 77.0 ± 19.6 pA 7 cells; LTP: baseline EPSC 74.6 ± 16.4 pA, 12 cells; Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.767; Spearman's Rank-Order correlation between the amplitude of EPSCs during baseline and 15–20 min after plasticity induction, p>0.05 for both comparisons).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis of baseline EPSC amplitudes and plasticity magnitude.

claim: The probability of failures in synaptic signaling increases by ~99% after LTD induction (from 15.5 ± 5.9% to 30.9 ± 11.3%; p=0.028).
source: The probability of failures in synaptic signaling increased by ~99% after LTD (15–20 min after aBFS; from 15.5 ± 5.9% to 30.9 ± 11.3%; 5 HIPP and two non-identified SOMIs; p=0.028, paired t-test) but declined by ~74% after LTP induction (from 15.8 ± 6.3% to 7.7 ± 4.2%; 11 HIL cells; p=0.016, Wilcoxon Signed Rank test; Figure 3—figure supplement 4A), pointing to its presynaptic origin.
evidence: Based on analysis of transmission failures in 7 cells showing LTD, pointing to presynaptic expression.

claim: The probability of failures in synaptic signaling declines by ~74% after LTP induction (from 15.8 ± 6.3% to 7.7 ± 4.2%; p=0.016).
source: The probability of failures in synaptic signaling increased by ~99% after LTD (15–20 min after aBFS; from 15.5 ± 5.9% to 30.9 ± 11.3%; 5 HIPP and two non-identified SOMIs; p=0.028, paired t-test) but declined by ~74% after LTP induction (from 15.8 ± 6.3% to 7.7 ± 4.2%; 11 HIL cells; p=0.016, Wilcoxon Signed Rank test; Figure 3—figure supplement 4A), pointing to its presynaptic origin.
evidence: Based on analysis of transmission failures in 11 HIL cells showing LTP, pointing to presynaptic expression.

claim: Coefficient-of-variation (CV) analysis indicates that both LTD and LTP are expressed at presynaptic sites.
source: Moreover, a plot of the CV−2 of the mean EPSC amplitude in the LTD and LTP phase, both normalized to baseline values, revealed that the majority of data points were located close or above the identity line for LTP and close to the identity line for LTD (17 cells in total; Figure 3—figure supplement 4B). These data indicate that both forms of plasticity changes are expressed at presynaptic sites.
evidence: Based on CV analysis of 17 cells showing plasticity.

claim: IPSCs recorded in granule cells have small peak amplitude and slow rise time independent of light-pulse location (amplitude IPSComl 9.6 ± 1.2 pA vs IPSCpsoma 8.7 ± 1.6 pA, p=0.4327; rise time IPSComl 1.8 ± 0.2 ms vs IPSCpsoma 2.5 ± 0.6 ms; p=0.2094).
source: IPSCs recorded in GCs had always a small peak amplitude and slow rise time independent on the light-pulse location (amplitude IPSComl9.6 ± 1.2 pA vs IPSCpsoma8.7 ± 1.6 pA, p=0.4327; Figure 4C; rise time IPSComl1.8 ± 0.2 ms vs IPSCpsoma2.5 ± 0.6 ms; p=0.2094, two-tailed Wilcoxon Rank Sum test) suggesting their distal dendritic origin.
evidence: Based on optogenetic experiments in 12 granule cells, suggesting distal dendritic origin of IPSCs.

claim: Distally induced IPSCs in interneurons are 6.9-fold smaller than those induced close to the soma (IPSComl 23.0 ± 6.4 pA vs IPSCpsoma 159.6 ± 72.5 pA, p=0.028).
source: On the contrary, distally induced IPSCs in interneurons, were 6.9-fold smaller than the ones induced close to the soma (IPSComl23.0 ± 6.4 pA vs IPSCpsoma159.6 ± 72.5 pA, p=0.028, paired Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; Figure 4B,C) and had a significantly slower rise time (IPSComl1.8 ± 0.6 ms vs IPSCpsoma0.7 ± 0.2 ms; p=0.046, paired Wilcoxon Rank Sum test), suggesting that in addition to dendritic inhibition, interneurons receive powerful perisomatic SOMI-mediated synaptic inhibition.
evidence: Based on optogenetic experiments in 6 interneurons, suggesting perisomatic inhibition.

claim: Distally induced IPSCs in interneurons have a significantly slower rise time than those induced close to the soma (IPSComl 1.8 ± 0.6 ms vs IPSCpsoma 0.7 ± 0.2 ms; p=0.046).
source: On the contrary, distally induced IPSCs in interneurons, were 6.9-fold smaller than the ones induced close to the soma (IPSComl23.0 ± 6.4 pA vs IPSCpsoma159.6 ± 72.5 pA, p=0.028, paired Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; Figure 4B,C) and had a significantly slower rise time (IPSComl1.8 ± 0.6 ms vs IPSCpsoma0.7 ± 0.2 ms; p=0.046, paired Wilcoxon Rank Sum test), suggesting that in addition to dendritic inhibition, interneurons receive powerful perisomatic SOMI-mediated synaptic inhibition.
evidence: Based on optogenetic experiments in 6 interneurons.

claim: High-resolution confocal images reveal SOM+ boutons at the soma of parvalbumin-expressing interneurons (PVIs).
source: Indeed, high-resolution confocal images revealed SOM+ boutons at the soma of PVIs (13 cells; Figure 4A, inset).
evidence: Based on confocal microscopy observations in 13 PVIs.

claim: Somatically evoked IPSCs in interneurons have a 3.4-fold faster rise time than those evoked in granule cells (p=0.0037).
source: Consistent with the proposed synapse location, somatically evoked IPSCs in interneurons had a 3.4-fold faster rise time and an 18.3-fold larger amplitude than the ones evoked in GCs (p=0.0037 and p=0.00074, respectively, Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; Figure 4D).
evidence: Based on optogenetic experiments comparing IPSCs in interneurons and granule cells.

claim: Somatically evoked IPSCs in interneurons have an 18.3-fold larger amplitude than those evoked in granule cells (p=0.00074).
source: Consistent with the proposed synapse location, somatically evoked IPSCs in interneurons had a 3.4-fold faster rise time and an 18.3-fold larger amplitude than the ones evoked in GCs (p=0.0037 and p=0.00074, respectively, Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; Figure 4D).
evidence: Based on optogenetic experiments comparing IPSCs in interneurons and granule cells.

claim: The amplitude ratio between IPSCpsoma and IPSComl is ~sixfold higher in interneurons than in granule cells (5.8 ± 1.3 vs 1.0 ± 0.2; p=0.000078).
source: This is further reflected in a ~sixfold higher amplitude ratio between IPSCpsoma and IPSComl in interneurons than in GCs (5.8 ± 1.3 vs 1.0 ± 0.2; p=0.000078, t-test; Figure 4D).
evidence: Based on optogenetic experiments comparing IPSCs in interneurons and granule cells.

claim: HIPP cells provide dendritic inhibition onto granule cells and interneurons.
source: Thus, HIPP cells provide dendritic inhibition onto GCs and interneurons, whereas SOM+ axons in the hilus seem to supply powerful perisomatic inhibition onto interneurons (Figure 4E).
evidence: Inferred from optogenetic experiments showing small, slow IPSCs in granule cells and location-independent properties.

claim: SOM+ axons in the hilus supply powerful perisomatic inhibition onto interneurons.
source: Thus, HIPP cells provide dendritic inhibition onto GCs and interneurons, whereas SOM+ axons in the hilus seem to supply powerful perisomatic inhibition onto interneurons (Figure 4E).
evidence: Inferred from optogenetic experiments showing large, fast perisomatic IPSCs in interneurons.

claim: Single action potentials in presynaptic HIL cells evoke unitary IPSCs (uIPSCs) in target interneurons after a short latency (1.6 ± 0.25 ms), with a fast rise time (0.6 ± 0.06 ms) and a fast decay time constant (τ = 11.2 ± 0.6 ms).
source: Single action potentials in presynaptic HILs evoked unitary IPSCs (uIPSCs) in target interneurons (two basket cells, two HILs; Figure 4F) after a short latency (1.6 ± 0.25 ms), with a fast rise time (0.6 ± 0.06 ms) and a fast decay time constant (τ = 11.2 ± 0.6 ms; Figure 4G).
evidence: Based on paired whole-cell recordings from 4 HIL-interneuron pairs.

claim: The amplitude of unitary IPSCs from HIL cells to interneurons is variable with a mean value of 59.1 ± 17.6 pA (range 23.4–91.8 pA).
source: The amplitude was variable with a mean value of 59.1 ± 17.6 pA (range 23.4–91.8 pA).
evidence: Based on paired whole-cell recordings from 4 HIL-interneuron pairs.

claim: HIL cells provide perisomatic inhibition to DG-interneurons including basket cells and HIL cells.
source: Thus, HILs provide perisomatic inhibition to DG-interneurons including basket cells and HILs.
evidence: Based on paired whole-cell recordings showing functional synaptic connections.

claim: Putative synaptic contacts formed by DG-septal SOMIs are identified at cell bodies or proximal dendrites of cholinergic cells and PVIs in the medial septum.
source: By using confocal microscopy, we identified putative synaptic contacts, defined as presynaptic SOM-GFP+ axon varicosities co-localizing gephyrin, a postsynaptic marker of GABAergic terminals (Alldred et al., 2005; Fritschy et al., 2008), in close proximity to cell bodies or proximal dendrites of cholinergic cells and PVIs (67 ChAT neurons tested in six slices, three mice; 126 PVIs tested in 13 slices; three mice; Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Based on confocal microscopy observations in 67 ChAT neurons and 126 PVIs from three mice, with gephyrin colocalization.

claim: SOM+ axonal fibers are observed in close vicinity of intracellularly labeled putative glutamatergic cells in the medial septum, but lack bouton-like shape and postsynaptic gephyrin expression.
source: In case of putative glutamatergic cells as defined by their discharge activity (Figure 5D, inset), we observed SOM+ axonal fibers in close vicinity of intracellularly labeled cell bodies or proximal dendrites. However, they lacked a bouton-like shape as well as postsynaptic gephyrin expression (23 cells tested; Figure 5D).
evidence: Based on confocal microscopy observations in 23 putative glutamatergic cells.

claim: Fast-spiking PVIs in the medial septum form 31% of the recorded neuron population and discharge action potentials with short half-duration (0.43 ± 0.02 ms) and high maximal frequency (191.2 ± 8.1 Hz).
source: Fast-spiking PVIs formed 31% of the recorded neuron population and discharged action potentials with short half-duration and high maximal frequency (half duration: 0.43 ± 0.02 ms; frequency: 191.2 ± 8.1 Hz; adaptation ratio: 1.8 ± 0.1, input resistance: 318.5 ± 40.3 MΩ, 32 cells; Figure 6A).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological characterization of 32 PVIs in the medial septum.

claim: Cholinergic cells (ChATs) in the medial septum form 47% of recorded cells and discharge action potentials with broader half-width (0.9 ± 0.03 ms), lower discharge frequency (32.8 ± 1.9 Hz), and larger adaptation of spike trains (5.3 ± 0.4) than PVIs (p<0.0001 for all three comparisons).
source: ChATs formed with 47% the majority of recorded cells (49 cells; Figure 6B) and discharged action potentials with a significantly broader half-width, lower discharge frequency and larger adaptation of spike trains than PVIs (half duration: 0.9 ± 0.03 ms; frequency: 32.8 ± 1.9 Hz; adaptation ratio: of 5.3 ± 0.4; p<0.0001 for all three pairwise comparisons; t-test; Figure 6B) consistent with previous reports (Markram and Segal, 1990).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological characterization of 49 ChAT cells, consistent with previous reports by Markram and Segal, 1990.

claim: Putative glutamatergic cells in the medial septum form 22% of recorded cells and generate bursts of action potentials characteristic for glutamatergic cells (half duration: 0.8 ± 0.06 ms; frequency: 35.8 ± 7.0 Hz; input resistance: 387.9 ± 42.7 MΩ).
source: The remaining 22% of the cells generated bursts of action potentials characteristic for glutamatergic cells (half duration: 0.8 ± 0.06 ms; frequency: 35.8 ± 7.0 Hz; input resistance: 387.9 ± 42.7 MΩ; 23 cells; Manseau et al., 2005; Huh et al. 2010; Figure 6C).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological characterization of 23 cells, consistent with previous reports by Manseau et al., 2005 and Huh et al., 2010.

claim: DG-septal projecting SOMIs provide the strongest inhibition onto putative glutamatergic neurons (237.0 ± 92.6 pA; 5 out of 23 tested cells).
source: Synaptic signals with the largest mean peak amplitude were obtained from putative glutamatergic neurons (237.0 ± 92.6 pA; 5 out of 23 tested cells; Figure 6D, bottom), whereas ~12.8 and ~7.0 times smaller IPSCs were recorded from PVIs and ChATs, respectively (PVI 18.5 ± 6.9 pA, 10 out of 32 tested cells; ChAT 33.8 ± 9.0 pA, 7 out of 49 tested cells; p<0.01 for both comparisons, Mann Whitney U test; Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on optogenetic experiments in 5 putative glutamatergic cells.

claim: DG-septal projecting SOMIs provide ~12.8 times weaker inhibition onto PVIs (18.5 ± 6.9 pA; 10 out of 32 tested cells) than onto putative glutamatergic neurons (p<0.01).
source: Synaptic signals with the largest mean peak amplitude were obtained from putative glutamatergic neurons (237.0 ± 92.6 pA; 5 out of 23 tested cells; Figure 6D, bottom), whereas ~12.8 and ~7.0 times smaller IPSCs were recorded from PVIs and ChATs, respectively (PVI 18.5 ± 6.9 pA, 10 out of 32 tested cells; ChAT 33.8 ± 9.0 pA, 7 out of 49 tested cells; p<0.01 for both comparisons, Mann Whitney U test; Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on optogenetic experiments in 10 PVIs.

claim: DG-septal projecting SOMIs provide ~7.0 times weaker inhibition onto ChAT cells (33.8 ± 9.0 pA; 7 out of 49 tested cells) than onto putative glutamatergic neurons (p<0.01).
source: Synaptic signals with the largest mean peak amplitude were obtained from putative glutamatergic neurons (237.0 ± 92.6 pA; 5 out of 23 tested cells; Figure 6D, bottom), whereas ~12.8 and ~7.0 times smaller IPSCs were recorded from PVIs and ChATs, respectively (PVI 18.5 ± 6.9 pA, 10 out of 32 tested cells; ChAT 33.8 ± 9.0 pA, 7 out of 49 tested cells; p<0.01 for both comparisons, Mann Whitney U test; Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on optogenetic experiments in 7 ChAT cells.

claim: IPSCs evoked by DG-septal SOMIs can be blocked by 10 µM SR95531 (98.3 ± 4.2% block), indicating their GABAA receptor-mediated nature.
source: IPSCs could be blocked by 10 µM SR95531 indicating their GABAA receptor-mediated nature (98.3 ± 4.2% block, 3 ChAT cells tested; Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on pharmacological experiments in 3 ChAT cells.

claim: The dentate gyrus contains at least two morphologically contrasting SOMI types: HIPP cells with axon fibers dispersing predominantly in the outer molecular layer and HIL cells with axon largely located in the hilus.
source: Thus, the DG contains at least two morphologically contrasting SOMI types, HIPP cells with axon fibers dispersing predominantly in the outer molecular layer and HIL cells, with axon largely located in the hilus.
evidence: Summary statement based on morphological reconstructions and analysis.

claim: HIPP cells are classical feedback inhibitory interneurons providing weak and slow dendritic inhibition onto granule cells and local interneurons.
source: We show that HIPP cells (Halasy and Somogyi, 1993; Han et al., 1993; Mott et al., 1997; Hosp et al., 2014) are classical feedback inhibitory interneurons providing weak and slow dendritic-inhibition onto GCs and local interneurons.
evidence: Based on optogenetic experiments showing weak, slow IPSCs and consistent with previous reports.

claim: HIL cells exert strong perisomatic inhibition onto local GABAergic inhibitory cells.
source: We identified a new DG-SOMI type, hilus-associated interneurons (HILs), with axon collaterals in the hilus. They exert strong perisomatic inhibition onto local GABAergic inhibitory cells.
evidence: Based on optogenetic and paired recording experiments showing strong, fast perisomatic IPSCs.

claim: HIL but not HIPP cells form long-range connections to the medial septum.
source: Moreover, HIL but not HIPP cells form long-range connections to the medial septum.
evidence: Based on retrograde tracing experiments showing that 86.7% of DG-septal cells are HIL cells.

claim: Repetitive activation of glutamatergic inputs onto HIPP cells induces long-lasting depression (LTD) of synaptic transmission.
source: Repetitive activation of glutamatergic inputs onto HIPP cells induces long-lasting-depression (LTD) of synaptic transmission but long-term-potentiation (LTP) of synaptic signals in HIL cells.
evidence: Based on plasticity experiments showing LTD in HIPP cells.

claim: Repetitive activation of glutamatergic inputs onto HIL cells induces long-term potentiation (LTP) of synaptic signals.
source: Repetitive activation of glutamatergic inputs onto HIPP cells induces long-lasting-depression (LTD) of synaptic transmission but long-term-potentiation (LTP) of synaptic signals in HIL cells.
evidence: Based on plasticity experiments showing LTP in HIL cells.

claim: LTD in HIPP cells may assist flow of spatial information from the entorhinal cortex to the dentate gyrus.
source: Thus, LTD in HIPPs may assist flow of spatial information from the entorhinal cortex to the DG, whereas LTP in HILs may facilitate the temporal coordination of GCs with activity patterns governed by the medial septum.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the functional role of LTD in HIPP cells.

claim: LTP in HIL cells may facilitate the temporal coordination of granule cells with activity patterns governed by the medial septum.
source: Thus, LTD in HIPPs may assist flow of spatial information from the entorhinal cortex to the DG, whereas LTP in HILs may facilitate the temporal coordination of GCs with activity patterns governed by the medial septum.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the functional role of LTP in HIL cells.

claim: The dentate gyrus plays an indispensable role in the formation of new memories and memory associations in various species including humans, nonhuman primates and rodents.
source: Together with the hippocampus, it plays an indispensable role in the formation of new memories and memory associations in various species including humans, nonhuman primates and rodents (Burgess et al., 2002; Leutgeb et al., 2005; Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004; Bakker et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge from multiple cited studies.

claim: The dentate gyrus translates rich input from the entorhinal cortex into sparse segregated ('orthogonalized') representations, a process called pattern separation.
source: It receives a rich multimodal input from the entorhinal cortex via the perforant path which carries information on various modalities of external cues and translates the rich input stream into sparse segregated ('orthogonalized') representations, a process called pattern separation (Marr, 1971; Treves and Rolls, 1994; Leutgeb et al., 2007; Kitamura et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge from multiple cited studies.

claim: Granule cell activity in the dentate gyrus is sparse.
source: Consistent with this theory, GC activity is sparse (Liu et al., 2012; Ramirez et al., 2013; Denny et al., 2014; Danielson et al., 2016) and governed by strong GABAergic inhibition (Nitz and McNaughton, 2004; Pernía-Andrade and Jonas, 2014).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge from multiple cited studies.

claim: Granule cell activity in the dentate gyrus is governed by strong GABAergic inhibition.
source: Consistent with this theory, GC activity is sparse (Liu et al., 2012; Ramirez et al., 2013; Denny et al., 2014; Danielson et al., 2016) and governed by strong GABAergic inhibition (Nitz and McNaughton, 2004; Pernía-Andrade and Jonas, 2014).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge from multiple cited studies.

claim: Parvalbumin-expressing interneurons (PVIs) receive convergent excitatory inputs from the perforant path at their apical dendrites and from local granule cells via their mossy fiber synapses at their basal dendrites.
source: PVIs receive convergent excitatory inputs from the perforant path at their apical dendrites and from local GCs via their mossy fiber synapses at their basal dendrites and provide powerful feedforward and feedback inhibition to large populations of GCs (Sambandan et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge from cited study by Sambandan et al., 2010.

claim: PVIs provide powerful feedforward and feedback inhibition to large populations of granule cells.
source: PVIs receive convergent excitatory inputs from the perforant path at their apical dendrites and from local GCs via their mossy fiber synapses at their basal dendrites and provide powerful feedforward and feedback inhibition to large populations of GCs (Sambandan et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge from cited study by Sambandan et al., 2010.

claim: HIPP cells have been considered to be synonymous for DG-SOMIs.
source: HIPP cells have so far been considered to be synonymous for DG-SOMIs (Freund and Buzsáki, 1996; Mott et al., 1997).
evidence: Based on previous scientific literature by Freund and Buzsáki, 1996 and Mott et al., 1997.

claim: SOM-positive axon fibers predominantly project in the outer half of the molecular layer, co-aligned with the perforant path.
source: Indeed, immunohistochemical investigations showed that SOM-positive axon fibers predominantly project in the outer half of the molecular layer, co-aligned with the perforant path (Halasy and Somogyi, 1993; Han et al., 1993; Mott et al., 1997; Hosp et al., 2014; Savanthrapadian et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge from multiple cited studies.

claim: Electron microscopical studies revealed SOM-expressing terminals at apical dendrites of granule cells and very likely interneurons in the dentate gyrus.
source: Moreover, electron microscopical studies revealed SOM-expressing terminals at apical dendrites of GCs and very likely interneurons in the DG (Leranth et al., 1990; Peng et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge from cited studies by Leranth et al., 1990 and Peng et al., 2013.

claim: HIPP cells are in the optimal position to control information flow from the entorhinal cortex via the dentate gyrus to the CA3 area by potentially influencing dendritic computation and synaptic plasticity.
source: Thus, HIPP cells are in the optimal position to control information flow from the entorhinal cortex via the DG to the CA3 area by potentially influencing dendritic computation and synaptic plasticity (Miles et al., 1996; Maccaferri, 2005).
evidence: Inferred from anatomical position and consistent with previous reports by Miles et al., 1996 and Maccaferri, 2005.

claim: Optogenetic silencing of DG-SOMIs resulted in the loss of granule cell engrams and spatial context recognition.
source: Consistent with this theory, optogenetic silencing of DG-SOMIs resulted in the loss of GC engrams and spatial context recognition (Stefanelli et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on cited study by Stefanelli et al., 2016.

claim: Cholinergic inputs from the medial septum are critical for the emergence of theta oscillations in the hippocampus and the dentate gyrus.
source: In the classical view, cholinergic inputs from the medial septum are critical for the emergence of theta oscillations in the hippocampus (Stewart and Fox, 1990) and the DG (Pabst et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge from cited studies by Stewart and Fox, 1990 and Pabst et al., 2016.

claim: Selective deletion of septal GABAergic cells resulted in a marked reduction of hippocampal theta power and spatial memory.
source: Indeed, selective deletion of septal GABAergic cells resulted in a marked reduction of hippocampal theta power (Yoder and Pang, 2005) and spatial memory (Pang et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on cited studies by Yoder and Pang, 2005 and Pang et al., 2011.

claim: Septal GABAergic cells contact exclusively interneurons in the hippocampus.
source: These GABAergic cells contact exclusively interneurons in the hippocampus (Gulyás et al., 1990; Borhegyi et al., 2004; Hangya et al., 2009; Hassani et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge from multiple cited studies.

claim: The major GABAergic route from the medial septum to the hippocampus is mediated by PVIs.
source: The major GABAergic route from the medial septum to the hippocampus is mediated by PVIs (Köhler et al., 1984; Tóth et al., 1993).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge from cited studies by Köhler et al., 1984 and Tóth et al., 1993.

claim: Septal PVIs target almost exclusively GABAergic cells in CA1 and CA3.
source: They have been shown to target almost exclusively GABAergic cells in CA1 and CA3 (Leranth et al., 1990; Unal et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge from cited studies by Leranth et al., 1990 and Unal et al., 2015.

claim: Most hippocampal-septal GABAergic targets are the source of back-projections to the medial septum, forming a bi-directional hippocampal-septal interneuron loop.
source: Most of these targets have been demonstrated to be the source of back-projections to the medial septum (Tóth et al., 1993; Takács et al., 2008) thereby forming a bi-directional hippocampal-septal interneuron loop.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge from cited studies by Tóth et al., 1993 and Takács et al., 2008.

claim: A bi-directional interneuron loop may exist between the dentate gyrus and the medial septum.
source: We propose that a bi-directional interneuron loop may also exist between the DG and the medial septum.
evidence: Proposed based on the finding that DG-septal cells are SOMIs and contact all main neuron types in the MSvDB.
